name: Mossy woods fragrances

card.summary: A woody subfamily of the fragrance wheel built around oakmoss and amber, used to give a person a deep, earthy, classic scent signature.
card.note: Oakmoss is a known skin sensitizer and is restricted in modern perfumery.

quick.overview:
Mossy woods is a subfamily in the Woody family of Michael Edwards's fragrance wheel, with oakmoss and amber as its defining notes. Scents here smell earthy, damp, deep and slightly sweet.

People choose fragrance as part of grooming: a scent signature adds to overall presentation and how a person is remembered. Mossy woods are one of the styles used for a classic, grounded impression. Controlled research on scent choice is general to fragrance, not specific to this subfamily.
quick.how: Fragrance is worn as a spray or cologne on skin and clothing. Shoppers browse by wheel family, picking mossy woods when they want an earthy, forest-floor character, often in classic chypre-type perfumes.
quick.risks: Oakmoss is a recognized contact allergen and its use is highly restricted by the International Fragrance Association, so many modern versions are reformulated with other materials. People with known fragrance sensitivities are advised to avoid it.

lead: Mossy woods is a subfamily of the Woody family on the fragrance wheel, alongside Woods (aromatic woods, vetiver) and Dry Woods (dry woods, leather). Its examples in Michael Edwards's wheel are oakmoss and amber, and classic chypres such as Guerlain's Mitsouko are placed in it.[1]

People use fragrance as a part of grooming and presentation, and the wheel is a tool for finding a style by family. Mossy woods give a deep, earthy, slightly sweet impression that wearers pair with a classic or outdoorsy image.[1][2]

Oakmoss, the lichen Evernia prunastri, is harvested in South-Central Europe and processed in Grasse, France, into absolutes used as fixatives and base notes in chypre and fougere perfumes. Its scent is described as woody, sharp and slightly sweet.[2]

angle.text: Mossy woods are one scent style a person can wear as part of their grooming. They add an olfactory impression of depth and classic character, rather than changing appearance itself.

paras: The fragrance wheel is a circular diagram showing relationships among scent groups, first published in 1949 by Paul Jellinek as the Odor Effects Diagram; Michael Edwards's version appeared in 1983 and 1992, and its Woods subgroups were added in 2008.[1] In the 2010 version, Woody splits into Woods, Mossy Woods and Dry Woods.[1]
Chypres span parts of the Woody and Oriental families and are hard to place; Mitsouko, a classic chypre, sits under Mossy Woods.[1]

Oakmoss absolutes act as fixatives and form the base of many fragrances and key components of fougere and chypre perfumes.[2] Use is highly restricted by IFRA standards, and many scents have been reformulated with substitutes. People with skin sensitization issues are advised to avoid it.[2]

timeline.event: Paul Jellinek publishes the first fragrance wheel.[1]
Michael Edwards publishes his Fragrance Wheel.[1]
Woods subgroups added to the wheel.[1]
Wheel revised; Mossy Woods sits in the Woody family.[1]
